utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to raise one matter regarding translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps request some guidance or assistance. According to our last check, Your Honour, we had 39 -- we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment until we get some peace. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We showed that there was still 39 exhibits on the notification lists of exhibits for Mr. Lazarevic which have not yet been translated. Right now I only know of one in particular that I may have some interest in using but I may not know until I have it translated. Regarding the next three witnesses Jelic, Filipovic, and Delic, we have 38 out of 45 for Jelic have not been translated; 15 of 16 for Filipovic have not been translated; and for Delic 92 out of 108. So for this witness and the next three we have some 184 outstanding documents to be translated. And I don't know if you can assist or intervene with CLSS for us once again, but that does seem to help when you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, can you assist on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Cepic, is dealing with that problem, but I can say that I'm sure that these documents have been sent to the CLSS for translation. I will check during the break what the situation is with the clerk or officer dealing with the translations and I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I saw intimation I think today or late yesterday to the effect that everything that had been submitted for translation by the Lazarevic Defence has been translated, although CLSS did expect to receive other material, which they haven't received and which may be the result of a change in plans for the presentation of the Defence. But my understanding at this minute is that everything you have submitted has been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was the priority list of evidence we wanted to use with Mr. Lazarevic, whereas Mr. Cepic has been looking at other evidence that I would like to use with the following witnesses. I really have to check with our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it dismays me to think that it may be that there is some interruption in the production line of material for translation in relation to your Defence, Mr. Bakrac, in view of all the efforts we've made to ensure that every assistance is being given to you. So I hope that you will be able to clarify the position, if not later today then first thing tomorrow. This can't be allowed to derail the progress of the case, in view of the amount of time and energy we have invested in trying to avoid any disruption caused by difficulties in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not want to be too rash in saying anything like I did last Friday. I don't think, though, that there is an interruption on our side in sending documents, but I will check all that and I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic, the cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The last thing in connection with the translations, if the Defence had decided not to use some of those that were originally noticed, if they will advise us of that, that will speed our preparations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, yesterday near the end of the day we were talking about that portion of your interview where you discussed that the MUP had certain VJ vehicles and equipment which they had not repainted blue, and you talked a little bit about the problem or the potential problem caused by that. I want to ask you, do you know with regard to that equipment you were talking about in your interview, did the MUP ever return all that equipment to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something I don't know because the highest level dealing with that kind of thing is the General Staff of the army, but even they were not able to make that kind of decision. It was the Ministry of Defence. So I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that leads to the next document I want to show you which is Exhibit 3D557, which is a VJ collegium meeting on the 3rd of December, 1998, and I've got a hard copy I can hand you that may assist. And for e-court I'm going to start at page 19 in the English, which I believe is also in e-court page 19. For you, General, on the hard copy I think it's page number 18 in your B/C/S. And I want to start with the portion where General Obradovic is talking. Have you found that? Yeah, I might have actually marked that in pink on your copy. And the fourth line town he talks about -- the fifth line it says: "Part of equipment to be Republic of Serbia MUP; a month ago we requested in writing the return of the equipment so that we could use it in the briefing." He's talking about a briefing regarding the Vienna Agreement. "MUP informed us today that they would not return that equipment. Actually it includes 20 personnel carriers and 23 mortars that are subject to the OSCE agreement." And he talks about the possible alternatives of whether it should be listed as being with the MUP or listed as being with the VJ and then the next paragraph he says: "Also, we have problems with two helicopters that the Serbian MUP has acquired. We are planning to present them as part of the army, but there is an opinion that it should be presented as being with the MUP." So from this it appears that at least in December 1998 there was still a problem about that equipment not being returned, and that's not inconsistent with what you answered before, that you don't know what happened to it, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat my previous answer, that I don't know what the General Staff is discussing here, I don't know whether the equipment was returned or not, but it doesn't look to me as contradictory to what I said, my knowledge at the time, and my knowledge to date does not allow me to answer differently. I don't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph General Grahovac is talking and he mentioned that: "An answer needs to be given now as to how the VJ has acquired MiG 24 helicopters. This is a big issue, the VJ will have to answer as to why they had to use the air force." General, were you aware that in December 1998 or before the VJ had MiG 24 helicopters?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, this looks like a typo. There are no helicopters MiG 24. This is a helicopter Mi 24. I answered this question yesterday I think. I was aware that a state security sector had one or two helicopters of that kind. I don't know whether they belonged to the arsenal of the army or they were perhaps the equipment of the unit for special operations, JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the army use helicopters in supporting MUP in any of those anti-terrorist operations in 1998 or 1999, before the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for medical evacuation. There were medical helicopters Mi8. From what I know, not a single Mi8 helicopter was used in combat or in anti-terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in English and, General, if you could go to I think the next page on your hard copy, you'll see that General Ojdanic says to put this problem on paper, and he'll try to bring it up first with the minister and then the FRY president. But I want to go down to General Dimitrijevic and on the B/C/S I think we'll have to scroll up to the bottom of the B/C/S page. General, do you know -- well, let me read this and ask you if you're -- have any information about it. He says: "Another detail from the statement with Clark and Solana where it says literally that after MUP forces withdraw from Kosovo, the heavy equipment and weapons are to be returned to the army, so MUP undertook to do it. The statement was signed by the FRY president, so what does this mean now that the minister of interior is allowed to say that we won't return it?" Were you aware that the -- part of the October agreements called for MUP to return to VJ any heavy equipment that it had borrowed or been loaned during 1998? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is fine with the question, but the wrong page is on the screen. You have the page in English, the right page, but we don't have the right page in Serbian. I think that should be taken care of. It is clear that there are no names such as Clark and Solana on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, that -- it appears we have the right page on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you recall my question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that and my answer is this: At that time all those statements regarding Clark and Solana were very remote for me, as were any discussions in the General Staff of the Ministry of Defence such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I understood that you did have some dealings with the OSCE verifiers. Were you not aware of this particular provision of the agreements regarding VJ equipment on loan to MUP? Is that something that you just didn't know about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that this whole discussion does not relate to the KVM mission in Kosovo, but to the Vienna Agreement between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the OSCE concerning control of conventional weapons under a special protocol, that's one thing. And second, I had one direct contact on the 4th of December with representative of the OSCE mission did not get me any information about that. I had occasion to see all the documentation available to the liaison team of the 3rd Army for OSCE, and this issue was never raised in all those documents. I simply never dealt with it as Chief of Staff of the corps and later commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the OSCE person with whom you had direct contact?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended a meeting which was also attended by Mr. Drewienkiewicz, as far as I remember, although I did not contribute anything to the discussion, I just attended as Chief of Staff of the corps; there was also a team from the army command and the corps command following that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think that's all I had for that particular collegium meeting. While I have those minutes in front of me, though, I'd like to ask you about one other -- and while I'm getting that document, that meeting you mentioned with that individual, is that in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean by attendance at the meeting with the OSCE mission, with the KVM in Pristina on the 4th December, Mr. Drewienkiewicz testified here about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, was that meeting in December?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was 4 December 1998. Maybe I am a bit off, but it must be in the transcript of Mr. Drewienkiewicz's testimony, he must have mentioned the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the reason I ask was I was trying to follow-up on our previous discussions about how many times you left Djakovica and the forward command post in 1998, and I recall you had mentioned meeting with OSCE but I thought you said something about October and that you had gone to a Joint Command meeting around that time. Can you help us with that? Was your meeting with OSCE one time and one time only, and that was in December?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once, and there was no meeting of the Joint Command in October that I attended. And as far as the OSCE is concerned, that meeting was on the 4th, with the proviso that the mission arrived in October, I had no contacts with them. Maybe the team from the corps was preparing to meet with them, I don't know about that. But we can find documents among the Defence exhibits and my Defence can show them. I cannot help any further now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the topics I had asked you about in connection with a couple of documents I showed you was whether or not you were aware of any problems or tension between General Pavkovic, as commander of the Pristina Corps at that time; and General Samardzic, commander of the 3rd Army. I want to direct your attention now to Exhibit 3D484, which is another meeting of the VJ collegium, this one on the 10th of December, 1998. And, General, I think this is page 14 in e-court in the B/C/S and it's page 14 of the English. And at the top of the page I will tell you that from the previous page that speaker is General Dimitrijevic. And four lines down in the English he says: "Number three, about the discrepancy between the Pristina Corps, the army, all the way to us here, that's obvious. I think that so many unusual incidents and a lot of what's going on in the Pristina Corps are precisely the consequence of, I am liberty to say, the alienation of the corps commander, and with him the command, from the VJ, both from the 3rd Army and the General Staff. True to the obvious inertia of the Kosovo heroes, they can now take it easy. If my information is correct, the corps commander has already been in Belgrade for two weeks, and of course things are going the way they are." First of all, let me ask you, as of the 10th of December do you know whether General Pavkovic had been in Belgrade for some time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I have nothing against the question, but with the reading. It's a problem with translation. As I said last time, it is better for Mr. Lazarevic to read the Serbian and then we could check whether the English is okay. I think generally it is not bad but in Serbian it says: "I am -- I'll take the liberty to say" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the -- could counsel please refer us to the section he's reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the interpreters are asking for you to refer them to the section that you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Third thing," line four, it begins with: "I'm saying in a way such a number of extraordinary events and a lot of things happening in the Pristina Corps are precisely a consequence I would be free to say in a certain way not of the alienation of the corps commander and the command around him from the VJ," so that there is a not before alienation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll have to get Mr. Lazarevic to read this, Mr. Hannis, because it appears to say exactly the opposite of what you put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I have a hard copy that I can hand him that may make it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I think if you'll go to the blue tab you'll get to the correct page, and I think the point that Mr. Fila was talking about, can you find the reference that he made?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you read that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Third, about this disagreement between the Pristina Corps and the army and us here, that's obvious. I think that even such a great number of extraordinary incidents and a lot of the things happening in the Pristina Corps are precisely a consequence, I would be free to say, of, in a way, not alienation of the corps commander and the corps command around him from the VJ." Should I read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's all we wanted to cover. Could you go to the next page -- well, first of all, my question was - I don't think you answered - do you know whether or not General Pavkovic was in Belgrade those -- sometime during -- for about ten days or two weeks around and before the 10th of December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the best goodwill, I still cannot answer that question. I can only say that I don't recall at all that the corps commander was absent from the corps and from the unit for more than two, three, or perhaps four days. I'm quite certain of that, and I'm seeing for the first time what is written here. I cannot say anything for a fact concerning this date of the 10th. The reference here to him being in Belgrade for two weeks now, I really can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's one matter dealt with, Mr. Hannis. As far as the actual content of the document is concerned, there does seem to be a problem with translation. I am certainly not clear on what the correct translation is, now having listened to three different versions. And we shall require you to submit this again for revision of the translation and to make a filing clarifying the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. I'll make a note. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, General, I'll move on to or move back to your interview. Now, during your interview one of the documents that Mr. Coo showed you is Exhibit P1423 which is a report from Colonel Curkovic about tasks carried out by the 15th Armoured Brigade. And you did comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Could I ask my colleague Mr. Hannis to give us the page reference because the general was given pages that he was supposed to take a look at and the pages in the transcript so we would like a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies. It's page 88 of the interview in Exhibit P950.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 88 is not on our list of what the questions would be about. We have page 67, that's the first page before that. We don't have page 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pages I indicated to them, I think the instruction also advised that starting at a particular page the General should watch for about five minutes from that point on to be sure that he captured everything we were including. I think if we'll look at the page references and look for about five minutes, this will be within the range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If this is a passage --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, Your Honours, the page that precedes 89 is 67, so I assume that from 67 to 88, because we looked at two pages and it took 12 minutes. I don't believe that it takes five minutes to cover 12 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document is listed at page 88. The questions and his answers about it appear at page 89, starting on line 19, which is on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if there's a particular issue over what was said in contrast to the evidence given here, then no doubt we will be able to identify the location and play it again, to avoid any suggestion that the witness has not had a fair opportunity to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, if we could look at that exhibit, I have a question for you concerning a reference to the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't want to look at the transcript right now; I would like to look at Exhibit P1423.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I can give you a hard copy. Now, you see the first reference to the Joint Command is under item number 1. "Between 25 July and 6 August 1998 MUP units were engaged by decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." When you were asked about this during the interview, page 89, line 19 - we'll play it if you need to, but let me ask you the question and you tell us if we need to - you said at line 22: "And the first part of the report where the brigade commander refers to the decision of the Joint Command, again I would like to point out to the fact that there is one sentence before this which both legally and de facto annuls this sentence. If you have a look at what is at the beginning of the document which reads: 'Pursuant to the document of the Pristina Corps command.'" Can you explain to me why you conclude that that legally annuls this sentence about the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explanation of this document pertains to the fact that the brigade commander is reporting to the corps commander. He's not reporting to the Joint Command. So he's referring to an order of the corps commander dated the 7th of August, and in accordance with that order, as specified there, he's supposed to provide answers. And in four items he provides answers to those questions in this report. Within the chain of command within the army system, this is the proper, regular reporting system that is in place. And I wanted to note at the time - and that's what I want to again note now - is that the brigade commander is reporting to the corps commander, referring to the corps commander's document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and it appears the brigade commander is reporting to the Pristina Corps command pursuant to a particular document 880-175. But how does that annul line 1 which says: "Between 25 July and 6 August ... That MUP units were engaged by a decision of the Joint Command" in certain activities? How do you conclude that? The request for a report from the Pristina Corps command could ask a subordinate to report about all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was giving that answer and now when I'm answering your question, what I had in mind was that the brigade commander was referring to a document that was unsigned and unstamped, that he had received from the corps command about actions in the time-period between the 25th of July and the 6th of August providing support to the MUP forces. And he explains those actions in which his unit provided support to the MUP forces, and those actions were carried out in accordance with the document that is entitled: The order of the Joint Command for the support to the MUP forces in such and such a time-period on such and such an axis. And he now explains this document that he had when he was carrying out these actions, and he is referring to it, that's the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, you told us that there was no Joint Command, and I'd like to know if you know what document in July or August 1998 is there or was there ordering these kind of operations. Because we don't have in our collection any Joint Command document ordering this operation, unsigned or otherwise, but you've just said now that he's responding to an unsigned, unstamped Joint Command document. So did you see that document in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two years ago, in the interview with the OTP investigator, I spoke about that. I said that I had seen some of those documents with the letterhead of the Joint Command that were not signed, and those documents pertained to the support for the MUP forces on the part of some Pristina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you're talking not only of the 16 or 17 from 1999, but you're also talking about some from 1998; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on at least three occasions I said that we had, so to speak, inherited that principle of providing support to the MUP forces from 1998. Whenever it was necessary to provide support to the MUP forces, documents were made in this format in order to indicate that those were combined operations where each element retained its own chain of command. So this was the gist of my answers in my testimony now and in my answers to the OTP investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I think you said just now that this brigade commander must be referring to some unsigned documents from the Joint Command in 1998 that came from the Pristina Corps command. How do you know that's where they came from? Did those also have Pristina Corps number on them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The log number of the Pristina Corps command is the first thing, and the second thing, maps were attached to those documents and other documents that were necessary for the task to be completed. And by your leave, Your Honours, I can tell you that I had an opportunity to see some of the documents from other brigade commanders who, in response to this document from the corps command, make no mention of the Joint Command at all, but simply refer to the decision of the Pristina Corps. This man made this kind of a reference and other commanders simply forgot, skipped this -- the name of this body, the Joint Command, because no such body existed as far as they were concerned with, only the corps existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the reference number was for Joint Command orders from the Pristina Corps in 1998, was it also the 455 or was it something different in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not 455, and let me be quite precise. 455 is the -- there are at least 300 ordinal numbers in the log-book that have nothing to do with the Joint Command, but as far as I know there are only 15 or 16 of them. But this is not a number from 1998, 455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I understand what we see here as your answer. You say: "There are at least 300 ordinal numbers in the log-book that have nothing to do with the Joint Command, but as far as I know there are only 15 or 16 of them." 15 or 16 what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The numbers under log number 455 where the Joint Command is used as a term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying 300 is the total of documents with the number 455 and only a small proportion are Joint Command documents; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour, in -- under this log-book. And there were dozens of other log numbers that do not mention what we're referring here as the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I think I understand now that in 1999, in the log-book for matters pertaining to 455 there were some 300 documents in total, correct so far, for Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're saying only 15 or 16 of those say "Joint Command" at the top with no reference to Pristina Corps, it just has: "Joint Command," then 455 dash something between 1 and 300?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Those are the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other documents related to 455 in 1999 in the Pristina Corps, what did they all have in common? How, if I'm the clerk keeping track of documents there, how would I know what to put in with a 455 number in front? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, and I actually tried to explain that a couple of days ago. Let me try to do it again. This is the log number of the cooperation organ -- of the operations organ, and that pertains to the operations organ in the corps command primarily and the contents may vary. Mostly this pertains to the use of the units in war and even before the war and some other activities, orders, taking protective measures, and so on. But the essence is that this is the log number of the operations organ in the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, immediately before the use of 455 as the number for the operations organ, what was the earlier number used by the operations organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I can remember as I sit here, the operations organ of the corps command had at least three or four other log numbers in addition to this one, at least, so different numbers, not 455. For instance, 692, that was for combat reports; 888 -- 880 for some other topics, so I can't really be accurate now, but there were at least three or four, probably even more of those numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I not right in saying, though, that we have before us number 455-1?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean before us in general, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm asking the witness if we have before us in evidence in this case 455-1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's from this list of documents, from this log-book, under this log number, that would be the first document from February 1999. And then until the end of the war they -- there were 300 other documents under that same log number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what was the trigger for activating this particular log number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the beginning of each calendar year, at the beginning of the calendar year, from the whole log-book of the corps command the command organs are given certain list of numbers, log numbers, for documents, and one of those was 455 for the operations organ. There was also 888, 692, and some other log numbers of this kind that were assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it, General, then between the 1st of the year 1999 and the 16th of February, that there was nothing that came up to trigger the use of 455 for the operations organ, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. From the 16th of February onwards, that log number was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're on this topic, let me pursue that a little bit. Can we look at Exhibit 5D276. And, General, I can give you a hard copy with the assistance of the usher. And this is a document dated the 22nd of March, 1999. It has the Pristina Corps number 455-55. I think you'll recall that also on the 22nd of March, 1999, we have two -- well, yeah, we have two Joint Command documents, P1966, which bears Pristina Corps number 455-56, the very next number in sequence after this one; and P1967, which has number 455-56/1, and that was the one that was your amendment and that was signed by you. Both of those, as I said, are also dated the 26th of March. Now, if you would look at this one, 5D276, we see it's a plan for execution of operation - and perhaps the word should be action - to rout Siptar terrorist forces in the sector of Donja Drenica and Gornji Lab to the 3rd Army commander personally, do you see that, signed by you, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this seems to be one of those actions against terrorists, and it appears that it's going to involve VJ forces and at least one element of the MUP with regard to the Gornji Lab sector. You'll see that in item 2.2. And this is to General Pavkovic you say this is "pursuant to your generalised proposal and specific plans." Do you recall now what General Pavkovic's generalised proposal and specific plans were regarding this document, this action?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, certainly. This document is related to a document dated the 16th of February, 1999, confidential number 455, that's the order to rout the terrorist forces in three flash-points. Once a signal is given without a date, this is the order that we've been discussing very frequently, and I think that this follows an order of the army commander dated the 1st of February, where he gives a certain time-period for the preparations and the planning. This is the sequence of events, the 1st of February, the 16th of February, and the 22nd of March, and this is the general concept that is -- that can be seen through all that. And the order of the army commander to prepare the plans, this is the 16-page plan, the order with the attachments. And now we start with the actual implementation, my proposal as to how to carry out this task, and there will be two or three other documents stemming from this one and they constantly have been causing confusion because they're entitled "the orders of the Joint Command." And we can see from this who is actually ordering -- issuing this order and what all this pertains to. Mr. Prosecutor, you're right, because 56 is the next number, that's the order of the Joint Command, that's the title of this next document. Because it pertains to the support to the MUP and it was called in such and such a way and this is causing all this confusion and making it impossible for us to understand what was actually going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you explain for us the difference -- why there's a difference between the format of this document, which is proposing an action in the Donja Drenica and Gornji Lab sectors, and those very specific and detailed orders we have for the actions in the Malo Kosovo area in Exhibits P1966 and 1967. Did General Pavkovic, after seeing this one, 5D276, tell you, No, no, no, I want something more specific and be sure and put "Joint Command" on the top? Why is there a difference between this document and those other two issued on the same day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us be quite precise. This is not an order. We are not talking about an order. So Mr. Hannis is misquoting. He says this is an order, but we can read or the General can read this is not an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, General, you should still answer the question asked to you by Mr. Hannis, to explain the difference between the format of this document and the other two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question. The difference is primarily in the type of document involved. There are combat documents for command and for reporting, and I don't want to list them any further, but this kind of document is a document whereby one proposes to the superior officer in accordance with the protocol that is quite strictly stipulated in the army in which an explanation is given for the concept as to how an action could be carried out. This is not an order. This is just a concept for the action. The army commander reads this document, but he does not only read it. He is given more detailed explanations, and then he decides whether to accept or not accept this. And only then are specific orders drafted. These are the orders for the use of the units. This is a completely different document, so this is where the difference is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, this has been clarified. I didn't want to make that suggestion. You see here in the translation on your screen that it says "plan," whereas in the Serbian we have the term concept, "zamisao," in Serbian, and I think that we have the correct translation now in the transcript, but we would just like to note that this is what it says in the document. Perhaps it would be of some use for us to hear the General read out the title of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can deal with that in re-examination. The term "concept" has already clearly appeared in the transcript. Are you departing from that document now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm going to go back and forth with it a little bit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, General, this is the concept for this action. Was there a similar document or documents for the Malo Kosovo actions that are detailed in Exhibits P1966 and your amendment, P1967? Was there some similar precursor document like this for that one?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a document related to Malo Kosovo, although the title is Gornji Lab, because it's not all of Malo Kosovo that it concerns. It describes a concept of an action in the area of Donja Drenica and Gornji Lab. And in point 2.2, the explanation relates specifically to the area of Gornji Lab.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But this document, 455-55, does not refer to the specific areas described in P1966 or 1967, does it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to have before me those documents as well in order to be accurate. I know specifically what this paper in front of me is. I have an idea about the other two documents, but I would like to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we then show the General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before then you move this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, there's a stamp on this in the top right-hand corner and there's handwriting immediately below the stamp. Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Precedes the orders of the Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why did you write that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In preparing my documents I wrote that in order to find the documents that accompany my order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then those documents were scanned and that's how it was scanned and how it came into e-court. And the preparation the General meant was proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I've mentioned to you before that it's not appropriate for you to try to explain things which a witness should be perfectly capable of explaining himself, and if you feel the need to clarify matters, then that's what re-examination is for. What we now have is your evidence, not the witness's evidence, about how this came to be; and that is quite inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really waited for the witness to answer himself, that it's signature and that he wrote it on the document we obtained in proofing. And then I added that because it was the only copy we got from the archives we were forced to scan it as such. So the witness did go first to explain how this note came to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, that is not so. You have the opportunity to resolve any outstanding issue like this in re-examination. Please do not do this again because it undermines the reliability of the explanation we're getting. It is not the way to go about clarifying things. My questions, I hope, are the simplest possible questions, and I do not think that this was a matter that would have caused you any difficulty to resolve in re-examination. I hope I'm not guilty of the five- or six-line questions that are such are a feature of this case other than occasionally. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I knew you were going to look at me after you said that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, is there anything else on this document that you wrote on after 1999, other than that comment about "precedes order of ZK," Joint Command? Is that the only thing you wrote on this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- I wrote a moment ago on my copy what you asked me about the "opsto," which is the municipal staff, and maybe this little cross, that meant to me that in proofing I should establish a link with the documents. The rest is not written by me. 1/2, I don't know what it means. The other numbers are from the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't write the number 57 that's in the circle or the handwritten 455-55 at the top?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. On most documents in the archives you will find 455 or some other number; the archivists wrote that. 57 must be a log number from the archives, and in my copy I also see some lines, some underlinings, the word "general" is underlined, for instance. I tried to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do we have a subsequent Joint Command order relating to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm going to get to that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I understood the process, this document, 5D276, was something that you would first send to General Pavkovic, and then after he approved it and advised you of approval, then one of those Joint Command orders with the 455 number would issue, like P1966 and P1967? Is that the process.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the process, but a document like this appears when between the prior document, plan, order, or whatever something changes between the concept and the realization. If we look at the document from February, there are three locations planned, Malisevo, Lab, and Drenica. Looking at the situation in the end of March, we in the corps command decided that we cannot perform this task in its entirety, that we were able to do only part of the task in Donja Drenica and Gornji Lab. So this is miniature version of that order 455-1. If it were not for that change, if that change didn't happen, then we would have proceeded to carry out the previous order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have the order of the 1st of February, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour. The 16th of February 45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, the first. Mr. Lazarevic said that this all -- the document we have on the screen related to a plan of the 16th of February, which was prepared following an order of the 1st of February. And I wondered if we had the 1st of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're referring to. I know that 455-1 is the 16th of February document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's likely to be the reference number on the one of the 1st of February? Is that a 3rd Army order rather than a Pristina Corps document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 3rd Army, Your Honour, in that document the commander of the army ordered that planning should be completed by 15th February, and we are now linking to 16 February, and on. My defence has shown the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I can tell you the number of that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D245.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, General, but I wanted to be clear. I understood that this document 5D276, I understand the correct translation should be concept. The concept first comes from you; and then it goes to General Pavkovic, the commander, for whatever action he deems appropriate to take; and once it's approved, then that was when some of these Joint Command orders were written up to detail task for the units that were going to participate in supporting the MUP in these anti-terrorist actions, correct? That's the time sequence, that's the steps you went through --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, next then I want to look at P21 -- I'm sorry, 2031. And, General, I have a hard copy of this one for you as well. This is dated also the 22nd of March, 1999, and this one is entitled "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" and it has that Pristina Corps number 455-54, the number immediately preceding the concept document we were just looking at. And this is a decision to crush and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the sector of Donja Drenica. So is this not a document that relates to the concept in 455-55?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents have been withdrawn from me. I would like them back to be able to compare. I need that to be able to give an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, we'll give you back the hard copy of 455-55.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're asking. This concept for executing the action is not sent by post, there is no time for that. And finally the forward command post of the army is at the command of the corps. That concept is taken there, I or the corps commander or I or my deputy goes, taking the map, and the document already prepared to execute that task. The army commander looks at all those three things, listens to the verbal rationale, we call it rationale. He gives his suggestions, if you have time enough, do this, do that, modify the decision, but this document relates to Donja Drenica in terms of time and in terms of the axes, as stated in the document 5D276. So the decision was prepared, the concept was prepared. The commander of the army was briefed, he approved it, and on the 24th the execution of the task began.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, you understand my puzzlement that it appears the decision at least is entered into the log with a lower number than the concept, which in terms of the process I understood would have preceded the decision. So why does the decision have the number 54, and I see it's typed in, and the concept has the number 455-55? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. On that same day both documents were created. It is quite possible and it's very likely the same person from the registry took both documents to be registered, and instead of registering 276 first, 2031 was logged before. This concept is an outline, but it is more elaborately shown in the decision. I believe that the concept was also reflected on the map. And at least three documents, those three documents were on the desk of the army commander when I was explaining to him, together with the operations officer, the concept, the idea, for performing that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you write anything on this document? I see there's the time and date for the operation has been written in by hand. Did you write that at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You will find that on a large number of documents of similar content. I don't know exactly who wrote that. This is an indication of readiness, when that has to be prepared. It's a document taken from the archives with that written in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1999, who would have filled in that information on this decision or a decision or order like this? Is that done by the commander or by somebody in the operations organ or whom would be the person responsible?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the rules it is the person who deals with these documents, but who precisely I don't know. In any case, it's the operations organ of the corps command. You see, this decision was not dated. Only when the commander of the army verified it, when he said, All right, I accept, this was probably written in by the operations officer, and that's when the implementation begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the 22nd of March, 1999, where were you physically located?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of March, I was at the command of the Pristina Corps in Pristina on our peacetime location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was General Pavkovic located on the 22nd of March, 1999? Was he also in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post in Pristina is in the barracks Kosovo Heroes, it's at the exit from Pristina to 3 kilometres away from the corps command. It was situated there beginning with the 2nd February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So on the 22nd of March, did you meet with him face-to-face to discuss any of these Joint Command orders or the actions contemplated by those orders?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot be sure at this moment, but it is highly likely that I personally explained the concept to the commander, accompanied by my operations officer; that would be the usual way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I notice that this decision begins with item number 4, the decision. We've seen many of these other documents where it has General -- usually the first three items, I think, number 1 is the enemy and number 2 is neighbours and 3 is the tasks for the Pristina Corps, for example. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are documents of both kinds. When a document starts with point 4, it would be a decision, whereas a complete order has points from 1 to the last. This decision follows from the 16th February document, describing in detail the forces of armed rebellion in the entire area of Drenica and Donja Drenica so that these points are missing from this document. In some documents they are complete, in others they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can tell, General, from the documents we've had on this subject matter for the 22nd of March, 1999, the only one I've seen so far that had items 1, 2, and 3 is P1966, the Joint Command order 455-56. Does that somehow mean that that was the master document for these others?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. As far as I can recall at this moment, other documents with the same heading include the first paragraph, whereas this document relates only to a small part called Malo Kosovo, especially point 1, the terrorist forces are not the same in Drenica as in Metohija. It cannot be an original document -- it cannot be the initial document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why do you say it cannot be? You mean the one on the screen in front of you now, 455-56?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document focuses primarily on Malo Kosovo in point 1. It gives a broader description of Siptar forces, but it concentrates on Malo Kosovo. It shows other hotbeds of crisis as well, but describes primarily Malo Kosovo and the units would concentrate on executing the task in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then how is it different from 455-54, the decision about the, I think, Donja Drenica area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a shortened order. It includes elements that the unit or units should execute beginning with paragraph 4 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell me why 455-56 is termed an order and 455-54 is a decision? What's the distinction, what's the difference, between those two terms in this context?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no major differences. Both documents are command documents, according to type. Both documents govern the use of units. The only difference in that document 154, the first paragraphs are omitted, own forces, neighbours, et cetera, and it begins with the enemy. Either there was not enough time or the engagement of units was minor so that it did not require that entire page to be written. That's simply the decision taken then to go with the abbreviated version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we can, and we shall resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I've got the impression from our interaction in the last few days that you are a bit of a stickler for precision and you've just answered that there were no major differences between using the term "order" and the term "decision." Isn't there some kind of -- within the army some distinction between those two terms?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having used the term "naredba" but "zapovest."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Both are interpreted as "order" into English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I used "decision." An order is a document that has a stipulated structure and a decision is part of the order from item 4 onwards; it is also a combat document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I see on the transcript an interpreter's note saying both "naredba" and "zapovest" are translated as order, but I'm not sure what word is used in Serbian to mean "decision" in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can the interpreters help me with that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We used "odluka."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "Odluka" is the Serbian word for decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I asked the question because for me in my brief experience in the army, if my commander said, I have decided, Private Hannis, that you're going to clean the latrine, it may not mean the same thing as if he said, I order you to clean the latrine. Is there no distinction between "odluka" and the terms "naredba" or "zapovest"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Zapovest," an order, as a combat document contains in item 4 the words "I have decided." It has the same wording, the same language is used in that item.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, General. I want to ask you about another document, and this will be Exhibit P -- 5D343. It's a one-page document that you should be able to see on the screen in a moment. It is from the command of the Pristina Corps signed by you, and I guess it's to the subordinate commanders requesting special combat reports. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And these reports appear related to tasks that have gone on previously, and I see handwritten here I guess it's under the word "urgent" has been translated in English as "communications with ZK," Joint Command. Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see the number for this is not in the 455 series, but this is 706-1. On the face of it, it looks to me like this is one that could easily go in the 455 series based on other documents we've seen. Can you tell us what this designated -- this 706 referred to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now we've come to the actual confirmation of what I have been saying. This is a demand in this order for reports on how the action on the 24th in Drenica had been carried out in accordance with the order of the Joint Command with the log number 455, but the operations officer did not enter it under that log number but under log number 706 because he has several log-book numbers at his disposal and he entered it under 706. So he did that. Just in technical terms, it may not have been the operations officer, the chief operations officer, because he would have entered it under 455, then it would bear the number 50-something, but this man entered it under log number 706 or perhaps the log-book operator just gave it this number because he was not paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So do you know who that individual would have been? Can you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I cannot, but my knowledge of that is as follows: I personally drafted this document, as you can see, and I requested that the commanders report to me, the operations officer took that to the log-book section. He left it there to be logged, and then it was supposed to be taken to be encrypted. This was a telegram, as you can see, because the signature is at the left-hand side, and probably it was somebody from the log-book section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if your signature's on the left-hand side of the page, this was a telegram; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in accordance with the Rules For Official Correspondence in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And because you've signed it, there was no need for that procedure we've seen on other documents regarding telegrams where a subordinate has the words "the telegram may be sent"; is that right? Is that why we don't see some other name below yours on this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the absence of the commander the person who is authorised to send a telegram enters a clause. The telegram may be sent and this person signs in lieu of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, did you get any of these requested reports by the 3rd of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did, certainly, most of them. I don't know whether I did by the 3rd of April, given the state of the communications system, but as a rule the units comply with the orders and if some units fail to submit those reports then couriers are sent or there is an additional request put in. But I cannot now claim whether they all had submitted their reports, but they were supposed to. I did saw some of the documents pertaining to those actions later on, and I think that we will actually all be able to see them in the course of our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would those special reports, special combat reports from your subordinate units in relation to this document make reference to this number, 706-1, they should, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should make reference to this number in order to be able to follow the sequence. Sometimes the subordinates forget to do so. They put in everything that needs to be put in but they fail to make the correct reference, but as a rule that's what they should do, they should refer to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. General, in case I forget, I'd like to ask you if in any future documents I show you if you've handwritten anything or made any notes on them, would you bring that to my attention if I fail to ask? Can you try and do that for me?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to look next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what exactly did you write under the word "urgent"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In connection with ZK," that's an abbreviation for the Joint Command, that's in relation to the previous document that we have just seen about Donja Drenica, so I indicated there was a link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did that a couple of months ago when we received the documents, when I personally went through some of the documents that the Defence had obtained in order to see to what extent those documents are linked with some previous ones and in order to establish the time-line during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I guess I'm not clear what it is about this document that made you write "communications with the Joint Command." Is it because you knew that the routing of the Siptar forces in the general area of Drenica was somehow related to the Joint Command? Because the words "Joint Command" don't appear in this typewritten document anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how it came on the translation, I'm not listening to English the translation, but in the transcript, it very clearly states "in connection with ZK," which is what the Serbian on the original, on the exhibit itself says. I don't know -- I'm trying to help Mr. Hannis, I don't know whether he's been led astray or what, but I don't know if that answers his question or addresses it, but I just wanted to make sure that he was aware of that, that that is the translation that is in the record based upon the reading by General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's at line 12, Mr. Hannis. It comes to the same thing I think in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, when you use the abbreviation "ZK" you were referring to Joint Command, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me, if I may answer your question before I forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a -- my preparation based on the analysis of the documents, and I wanted to note for my Defence counsel that they should find documents that should establish this sequence of events in a consistent manner because, by your leave, Your Honours, to be quite clear and to clarify this confusion, there is a document from the 3rd Army commander in which he orders the corps commander and then the corps commander orders something. And all of a sudden we have a document that is unsigned from the Joint Command and then we have another document from the corps commander and my idea, my view, what I know -- actually, what I was trying to do is I tried to help the Trial Chamber to see what is what. And this is what I had in mind when I made this notation, when I made notations of this kind on the edges of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Continuing with some of my questions about the numbering system, could we look at Exhibit P213. General, this is an order from Colonel Zivanovic apparently to his subordinate. It's entitled: "Ban on operations." Let me hand you a hard copy while we're looking for it. Did I give the wrong number? I meant to be 2113. My apologies. 2113, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've seen this document before I believe.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document in 2005 during my interview with the investigators, the OTP, I was shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see Colonel Zivanovic under the heading it says: "Pursuant to the order of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, strictly confidential number 1104-6 of 6 July 1998 ..." Can you tell us anything about what that says to you, and I mean the four-digit number, 1104. In other documents we've seen four-digit numbers coming from the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff. Do you know what body 1104 might pertain to or what level if it's somebody within the army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not pertain to the level of command, it pertains to the log number and my knowledge from that period is that this is the log number of the Pristina Corps command from 1998. And in this document, the support two MUP forces by certain corps combat groups was defined. This has nothing to do with the strategic level of command or the level of command in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's maybe my misunderstanding. Earlier you gave us some examples of some numbers used in the Pristina Corps, and I thought they were all three-digit numbers. Do you know who in the Pristina Corps command would have been dealing with 1104? Would that have been in the operations organs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the operations organ in 1998, in Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your interview when you spoke about this document at page 93 you had a comment about this brigade commander at line 9, based on reviewing what is written in this document you said: "This brigade would have to take the exam twice, but this is my response because I remember there was this map which went around and I believe everybody took it for granted and referred to it." First of all, Colonel Zivanovic in 1999 was one of your subordinates, right? He was the commander of the -- was it the 125th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in 1999 and also in 1998. He was also the Chief of Staff in that same brigade in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you became his superior, you didn't send him back for any remedial school, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And he's prohibiting the execution of any operations without the approval of the Joint Command and his own approval. That's July 1998. So, General, now we've seen references to the Joint Command as early as July 1998 from a brigade commander or -- was he lower at this time? Was he at a lower level?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here he's signing as the brigade commander. Now, whether he took over the duty of the brigade commander at that time, I don't know, but he was the Chief of Staff, that's for sure. But he is signed here as the brigade commander. Now, if I may answer the first question, why this reference, if I understand your question correctly, to the Joint Command in June [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: July, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw a document from General Samardzic, the 3rd Army commander, here in court a few days ago, where he prohibits that the support be given to the MUP forces by the Pristina Corps units if those requests are not all brought together at the MUP staff in Pristina level and then if the Pristina Corps or the 3rd Army has not approved this support. And now if this refers to this order of the 3rd Army commander and this term "the Joint Command" was forged to refer to the cooperation and coordination and support between the army and the MUP forces as early as in early July. I don't know when this term was forged or who actually came up with it, but this is my explanation for why on the 7th of July this commander is referring to such an order. So the army cannot support the MUP without the MUP staff putting in their request and without the 3rd Army or the Pristina Corps approving it, and somebody termed that the Joint Command, this kind of cooperation at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General -- and you didn't do any of the handwriting on this document, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have told you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look next at Exhibit 5D211. And, General, I believe this is a -- I don't have a hard copy for you so we'll have to look at the screen for this one. This is a combat report from the 11th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to item 2 I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I'm looking for a reference that talks about what the -- this is a combat report, on the first page it's directed to the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, I guess we have to go to page 3 of the English. Well, I'm having trouble finding the reference. There was a -- I believe it is the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm trying to find a reference to the plan for continued task -- well -- focal activities for the next day. Perhaps it's under item 8. I'm sorry, I can't read my note, Your Honour. Yes. And if we could go to that item in the B/C/S, I believe it's the next-to-the-last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a reference in the English to: "Engineer works in the zones of defence and the break-up of the remaining Siptar terrorist forces in the villages of Donje Obrinje and Mount Kosmac." Do you see that, I think it's at the very bottom?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a combat report signed by you and the actions in connection with Donje Obrinje and Mount Kosmac are referred to in the Joint Command order in exhibit P1970, which is 455-132. If you'll accept my word for that we can look at it in a minute, but I wanted to ask you this combat report is directed only to the 3rd Army command; and we had seen other combat reports before that time and some after that time which are sent to both the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command Staff. Isn't that correct, that for at least some period of time you were double reporting to the Supreme Command Staff and the 3rd Army? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the interpretation "double reporting." It's the same report sent to two addresses, to the command of the 3rd Army and to the Supreme Command Staff. Maybe I should have written "for their information," but sometimes it wasn't written. At one point the report was CC'd, but it's the same report, it's not two reports, one and the same report sent to two addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. When were you first asked to do that or is that something you did voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There exist volunteers in the army, but for activities like this -- it's not about voluntary or not voluntary. I cannot remember who ordered it. It was only the Supreme Command Staff that could have ordered it to the 3rd Army commander, and then he would have ordered it to me, but it was not a particular problem. It was maybe a problem for those who did the encrypting and the encoding, but I am not the one who suggested the addressees' list, whether they should go to the Supreme Command Staff or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did that requirement ever end before the war ended or were you required to do that throughout?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, those reports were sent throughout the war. Maybe I am wrong, maybe at some point it was ordered it was not needed anymore, but I believe it was sent this way until the end of the war, around the 12th of April it started I believe, but I didn't really check the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Could we look at the first page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the time, General, it appears that this one went only to the 3rd Army command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the 11th of April. Only the 3rd Army command is indicated. I hope the Trial Chamber will allow me another ten seconds to explain. You see the log number is 692, again from the operations organ, the operations organ had five or six log numbers. I wanted to point out this additional log number, but on the 11th of April this report went only to the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, with regard to the Joint Command operations actions that we have seen in evidence in this case, I want to refer you to Exhibit 5D373. This is a Pristina Corps document. It appears to have your signature and it's dated the 23rd of April, 1999. Now, General, this is entitled "effects of breaking Siptar terrorist forces, request for analysis," and this one we see is in the 455 series. My question is, I guess: This one, whoever was taking the information down for the log-book got it right this time and gave it a number in the 455 series instead of the 706 series; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see Colonel Ratko Tesevic was the one who deals with this document. He knows this topic, this subject matter, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who do the other initials pertain to above your name?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates the name of the typist at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this refers to operations or actions in certain areas, and I would indicate to you, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to save time, Your Honours, I would indicate that Zastric is referred to in exhibit P1977; Drenica Lipovaca is in P1974 and 1972; Zegovac in P1971; Zlas in P1973; Rugovo in P1878; Bajgora in P1975; Jezerce in P1976; and Kosmac in P1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, so with the exception I think of Cicavica, all these actions described here were the subject of Joint Command orders. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the point I have been trying to make. I as corps commander am asking the subordinate units to report to me about these operations that had one document titled "Joint Command," and it's clear that there is no Joint Command commanding, it's the corps command. You just enumerated all these operations that have the same heading "Joint Command." However, the system of command is such that the corps commander and brigade commanders exercised command. This is another piece of evidence that shows how the command really functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, would you look next at Exhibit 5D194. This is another Pristina Corps command document, it appears to have your signature dated the 15th of April, 1999, to the 3rd Army command, personally to the Chief of Staff. And I would like to ask you to read one of the paragraphs for me because I'm having some difficulty understanding the English, and I want to be sure it's not a matter of translation.
