Can you see the paragraph that talks about: "At 0800 hours on 18 April," I think it's the second one. Would you read that for us.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On 18 April 1999 at 0800 hours, the command of the Pristina Corps in coordinated action with the forces of the MUP of Serbian started an operation to crush and destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the said sector." It would be more accurate if it read: Shall launch, because the document is dated 15 April and it is written that the action or operation would start on the 18th of April at 0800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, that's precisely my question. The document is dated the 15th of April, and it seemed to be using the past tense for something that is dated three days in the future. Do you know how that happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the Trial Chamber, the word "starts" is in the present tense, otherwise it would have read "started" or "launched." In Serbian "starts" indicates an intention to start. It's actually describing a future action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read the next sentence for me. It starts with: "Pristina Corps forces ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The forces of the Pristina Corps set up a blockade on the line hydro-power station Radovac-Bresotvik village-Markova Pecina." I read this to mean that I am explaining to the army commander the concept of this operation that would be again accompanied by that unfortunate memorandum of the Joint Command and that coordinated action will be needed, but it is only in that sense that these sentences are correct, because the following passages tell us that I am requesting them to ensure coordinated action with the Podgorica Corps of the 2nd Army for the purposes of this operation, something that had been ordered before by the Chief of the General Staff. Look at the last sentence. Nothing had happened yet, it is about to happen. I am suggesting to the army commander to ensure coordinated action for the purposes of this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. General, in your answer you said at line 11: I am explaining to the commander the operation that would be accompanied by that unfortunate memorandum of the Joint Command." There's no mention of Joint Command in here. Is that because -- did you give that answer because you know this action relates to the one that is described in Exhibit P1878, which is Pristina Corps number 455-148, the number immediately preceding this one?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I know that because many documents are tied to this Rugova gorge and many of them have the same letterhead and only ten do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that 455-148, P1878, is the one that is linked to in General Ojdanic's suggestions in Exhibit P1487, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it follows that sequence. I could answer yes, but I believe you would -- at least I hope you would allow me to see it more specifically. Those are the Rugova gorge events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if light of what was read, I would request that the Defence submit this one for amended translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which part are you referring to in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the 0800 hours says launched and I think he indicated that should read "will launch" or "shall launch." And the next one is translated as "now as Pristina Corps forces are blocking," and it wasn't clear to me whether he was saying that was in the present tense or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in the end Mr. Lazarevic in relation to the second paragraph said it was in the present tense, launches an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, since you request it, Mr. Hannis, we shall instruct Mr. Bakrac to submit these two paragraphs for revision and to file the resultant clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, paragraph 2 -- but let me check, what is the other paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next one, paragraph 3, the words are "blocking." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to move on to a different topic for a moment now. In your interview there was some discussion about volunteers and conscripts. You mentioned that 120 were dismissed because you and the Pristina Corps weren't satisfied with their appearance and their conduct in the unit. Do you recall when that was, when that happened approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I be allowed to clarify the question? Are you asking about my interview with the Prosecution or the answer I gave here in my testimony about the number of volunteers who were turned back?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm -- either one if it happened at the same time. Was there more than one incident that you recall wherein volunteers were turned back?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained that volunteers were turned back and dismissed from the units of the Pristina Corps for at least three reasons. The first possibility that by their own admission they were not physically able to withstand the strain and the physical demands, and I showed an example wherein over a hundred were dismissed at their own request --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me -- okay.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I remember that at the beginning of the war, sometime in early April, the first group of volunteers were arrested for various misdeeds, including one part of them who did not personally participate in those offences, but that group, 32 of them, did not comply in terms of conduct and appearance and they were also turned back. And some were directed to appear before a medical panel to decide to what extent and how many of them could remain, but I remember that at the beginning of the war 32 of them were dismissed for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall seeing one of the exhibits from the evening briefings of the Supreme Command Staff where that event involving dismissal of some 32 volunteers was discussed at the level of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right, I accept that, but -- because that report went through the army command to the level of the General Staff, and I remember we had testimony about that and we had evidence shown. But I also remember the corps commands report about that, it was the 3rd or the 4th of April perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you next Exhibit 5D315. General, this is a document signed by you. It's dated the 10th of May, 1999, and it's talking about problems with some conscripts -- it says: "Conscripts in the reserve who were unfit for military service for mental reasons, but who covered up their state of health and enrolled as volunteers. Among conscripts as well as among soldiers of the March and September 1998 contingent." Now, first of all, I'm a little bit confused about that. I'm still a bit confused between conscripts and volunteers. But in either event, before those individuals would go on the line to be in active duty, I understood that there were procedures in place for psychological testing before they were received into the army and put to work; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. A volunteer becomes a military conscript once he is admitted into the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it sounds here as though as even as late as the 10th of May, 1999, you were having some problems with some of these guys with mental problems getting through the system and getting into the army and then having problems with abuse of weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document that I wrote, if you read it all, indicates, I believe, a general problem rather than something that was getting through the control system. It says, rather, that the whole wartime situation is affecting the mental status of those people who arrived as volunteers, apparently ready for difficult missions, but even those from the March contingent who had already been through difficult trials. I am describing these problems that are affecting the soldiers who have been through these difficulties and very hard experiences. I'm saying they should be sent before the medical board and given some assistance in overcoming these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to switch to another topic now. In your evidence you were shown Exhibit 5D383 by Mr. Bakrac I believe, and that is a 27 April 1999 document from the 3rd Army to command -- to the Pristina Corps command, notifying you that they were sending a forensic pathologist. But what I want to show you is the document that's referred to in 5D383, which we can see at 5D379, which is your original request that generated this sending of a pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see some handwriting in the top. Did you write any of that handwritten stuff on this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's a request for pathologist, and in the body of the text it says: "Due to the demonstrated need for exhumation and professional processing of bodies buried in graves on the Pristina Corps territory, where the persons who carried out the clearing of the bodies are unknown and there are indications that members of the army were responsible, we request that you urgently assign an appropriate expert-military forensic pathologist." What were the indications that you had that members of the army were responsible for some of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command did not have precise, concrete indications. This is a reference to the fact that in that area, in the broader surroundings, there were positions of the army. In my request, and this is my second personal initiative of this kind, I asked the first and the second superior command to send us forensic experts so that even then during the war we could make an on-site investigation, do the exhumation, and prevent a cover-up of the crime, if any. That was done on several occasions. Let me draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that in 2005 one of these locations was dealt with by UNMIK in Kosovo and Metohija and it had nothing to do with the army, but we did exhumations even during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, the question was a very specific question, and it relates to something you have written. And you have written that there are indications that members of the army were responsible. And the question was: What were these indications? Rightly or wrongly, there may be absolutely no foundation in them, but what were the indications that led you to make that specific statement in your request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information obtained concerning several locations came indirectly from several sources, from local residents, from unidentified persons, through the MUP specifically I remember it was the case in Lipljan and reached the corps command. And when these first reports came, the local residents were unable to distinguish between different armies. Anybody who carries weapons to him is a soldier. So this had to do with the first reports, and I want to say that we worked together with the MUP to investigate based on those initial reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you -- allowing that you don't know whether any of that VJ equipment was returned by the MUP, is it possible that some of these reports suggesting that the army was responsible really related to MUP using VJ vehicles and equipment?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I'm merely allowing myself a certain degree of latitude. A hundred Prosecution witnesses who testified here were not able to recognise things. They were talking about tanks with three barrels, army troops with the words "police" written on their backs --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, we didn't have a hundred witnesses testifying about that kind of thing; you're exaggerating and you know it. So I think you answered my question that you're allowing for that possibility. Let me go back to your earlier answer. You said: "The information obtained covering -- concerning several locations came indirectly from several sources." Do you have any idea of the number of bodies that you're talking about in this document? Was it ten or a hundred or 500?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that in late April, on the 26th, there were two locations in the Lipljan municipality where the pathologist and the forensic medicine specialist from the military medical academy exhumed 36 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the other bodies that related to this request for a pathologist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two requests for the involvement of the forensic medicine specialists, and as far as I know that was for six locations in Kosovo and Metohija. That's where the excerpts -- experts from the Army of Yugoslavia were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you wrote this on the 26th of April, did you have information or indication that there were bodies buried in the area of Izbica, and for which members of the army might have been involved?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I've already said, and let me repeat, this refers to the area of the municipality of Lipljan, and Izbica is either in Srbica or Glogovac, one of the two municipalities. And the army did not carry out any exhumations in Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't hear the testimony of Dr. Tomasevic? Didn't she talk about exhumations in the area of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did speak about that, but the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica issued an order, and it was in charge of that process. She was in Mitrovica as an expert to analyse the mortal remains on the request of the civilian bodies, not of the army. And no army personnel had been ordered by the relevant command to participate in the exhumation and the examination of the mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I want to talk some more about the numbering of Pristina Corps documents in the 455 series. This relates to -- I'll start with your 24 May 1999 report on noncompliance with the order on resubordination of the MUP. This is -- well, this exhibit is in evidence with two or three different numbers. I think it is in P1458.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe this same document has been referred to variously as Exhibit P1723 and it's also in I believe 1504. But I believe most recently it was referred to as Exhibit P1723.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if we could bring that up, General, you'll recall this one, yes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the Pristina Corps number is 455-172/2. Does that mean -- is this the second or is this the third document relating to the subject matter that would have been in the original, 455-172? Does that question make sense?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it makes sense if the procedure was complied with, then it does make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I have not seen a document 455-172/1, but on the 20th of April we have your exhibit 455-172 -- actually, we have two documents, one is P1504, if we could take a look at that. And this appears to be that order. You're passing on basically the Supreme Command order and the 3rd Army order about subordinating MUP units, correct? Do you recall that one?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, is that your signature in the bottom, bottom left?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the top of the document on the right there's something handwritten. Can you tell us what that says?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To the MUP staff in Pristina."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, probably somebody either in the logging section or in the operations organ, whoever was supposed to hand this document to the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we next look at Exhibit P -- or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell from the document which archive it has come from? Can you scroll it to the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The stamp in the right-hand side -- well, there are two stamps, one is above and one is below the address and it should assist me to tell you whether this had come from the central archives of the Army of Yugoslavia or from the previous archive where it was kept of the corps command archive. I can't do that because the stamps are illegible. Perhaps we might want to zoom-in and then we can try. No, I'm not able to identify the stamps. There are two stamps. I know that the documents from the central archive have stamps either in the upper right-hand corner or the lower right-hand corner, but here it is illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you even say that it's an army archive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm talking about the central archive of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the stamp or stamps that are on this, can you say for sure that these are army archive stamps or could this possibly have come from a MUP archive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really can't see what it says here. To be quite frank, I haven't seen the MUP stamp so I really couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're still there, General, can you tell us what's handwritten at the bottom? Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read the first word. The second word just behind the -- after the dash, it says it was not sent to some of the units. The document was not sent to some of the units, probably of -- because of a breakdown in communications, but I really can't read what the rest of it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And handwritten to the left it looks like it's a number like 1611 or 1615 with a line drawn toward 192. Is that a time indication?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this figure here, 16 hours 15 minutes indicates that this is when the telegrams were received in the engineering regiment and another unit. It is listed here all the units that the telegram was sent to, and it is visible from here that the telegram was not sent to some of the units because the communication lines were down, that's 16 hours 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we next look at Exhibit 5D370. General, this will be another document dated the 20th of April, 1999, from the Pristina Corps command. It appears to have your signature and a stamp in the lower left, and it too, it also, bears the number 455-172 but this is dealing with the request from the command of the 549th Motorised Brigade regarding a local commune forming a company and perhaps providing weapons. Why is it there are two documents from the Pristina Corps with the identical number, 455-172, on the 20th of April, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that a mistake was made here, and now as to why this mistake occurred, my theory is as following: As a rule, when a document is being processed, the corps command and log-book number are not entered, but a clear space is left for the stamp. And once it is taken to the log-book section of the registry, then this information is entered. Whoever processed this document looked at the list of the documents or didn't and made a mistake, entering two documents that are quite clearly completely different under the same number. This was probably corrected in the registry or log-book section once it was taken there and it was entered under the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the registry or the log-book would help us see which one of these is the correct 455-72 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both documents are correct, but it is impossible for both of them to be entered under the same number, 170, in the corps log-book. One of them should have been given a different number or another number should have been added to it, like let's say -1 or -2 in order to be able to distinguish between the two. But the documents as documents as such, are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we've seen now two documents -- two separate documents numbered 455-172 from the 20th of April and we have seen your 24 May 1999 report about the lack of resubordinating or the failure to resubordinate the MUP, which is number 455-172/2. Can you tell us what number 17 -- 455-172/1 is? Have you ever seen it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see, I didn't do any research into that, but of the two documents on the screen -- well, one of them was given a prefix 1 in the registry, and the next one, that's my assumption, that is related to the resubordination of MUP was then given the prefix, the additional number 2. And this is how we came to get the document 172/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But as I understood your answer before, there should be a 172/1, right? Wasn't that your explanation to me?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that out of those two documents, one of them had to be given the additional number 1 in the registry. So the one to the right is 172 and the other one is 172/1 and the next one that deals with the same topic is 170/2 [as interpreted] because they couldn't be entered in the log-book under the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right, but you told me those two documents from the 20th of April are totally unrelated. So if I understand you correctly, one of them should not have a 455-172 number. They have nothing to do with each other, do they, this one that talks about --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. That's right. That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it would help us understand if we had the log-book, wouldn't it? If we saw the log-book, we would see how these two documents on the 20th were entered into it, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where is that log-book?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The log-book is in the central archives of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you not able to get access to it when you were preparing your Defence case?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, it's never really occurred to me to look at the log-book, but we asked for the document to be given to us by the central archives based on their contents because who would have done that? The trial had already started and we had yet to receive the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I try to understand why these documents with identical numbers are a month apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe they're both the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but we then have 455-172/2 is dated the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, why is that -- why do they bear the same starting number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they deal with the things that happened on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the one that's dated the 24th of May and is numbered 455-172/2, how does that fit into the registry sequence when it's a month and four days later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That document -- the basic document has at least three or four empty spaces for supplementary documents, subdocuments, and then the first next document has the next following prefix that deals with -- if it deals with the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not really a pattern we've seen so far, is it, in these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would direct your attention to generally the evidence of a couple of witnesses for the Ojdanic Defence, who talked about the numbering of documents in connection with that General Pavkovic report dated the 25th of May and how that document that related to -- well, I don't want to testify. Maybe we need to find you that testimony, but I think it would help enlighten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, if you're content with the explanation, Mr. Hannis, then we need not spend time on it just now. It's time to break again, so we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to have a better reference for you in the morning regarding the testimony I thought I remembered about the numbering system from one or more of the Ojdanic Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, General, perhaps you can help us. It was my understanding from some of the prior evidence that the situations in which a number was issued with what I call a slash, I think Judge Bonomy refers to as a stroke, is a situation where the document is so closely related that there should be such a reference made. Sometimes it's a direct response to, for example, a request for information. Do you understand my question? Can you explain to us the circumstances under which a number such as 455-172 would have a slash and some related document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the subject matter or the activities covered or the contents of the document in general relates to the period that follows, if the contents is similar, related, then the next document gets a number after a slash or a stroke. It has to do with the similarity in content, the relevance between the one document and the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. General, on the 24th and 25th of May, where were you physically located? Were you in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24 and 25th May 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not in Pristina. Maybe in the broader area of Pristina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what's your definition of the broader area of Pristina? You're talking about within a radius of 10 kilometres or?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean outside the urban centre, I mean the locations where the corps command had set up it elements of follow-up command posts, next command posts. In Pristina there was only one such element I believe on the 28th of April we reached that location. We spent one day, or two days there, and moved on to do reconnaissance around Kosovo Polje and we have shown those documents here. That's why I am saying I was not in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was General Pavkovic at that time, was he with you? Were you two together on those dates?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the forward command post of the army was -- it's called the command post of the Pristina Corps. It doesn't mean being physically there. It means being in one of those installations, there were several buildings, or maybe in the immediate vicinity. As far as General Pavkovic is concerned, I don't always know where I was, let alone him. We were together or close to each other very often but I don't know about those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thought you had said earlier in your testimony that you were together much of the time. You don't recall whether you were with him on either the 24th or 25th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just confirmed it, but I really cannot, no matter how hard I try to tell you exactly where I was on the 24th or the 25th of May or where General Pavkovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you did a pretty good job of telling us where you were on the 26th, 27th, and 28th of April, but you can't tell us where you were on the 24th and 25th of May and whether or not General Pavkovic was with you on either of those dates; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that because in some documents it is written where I was because some of those situations, some of those days are memorable, others are not. And when I mentioned some other dates, I did not speak off the top of my head, I referred to documents. If there is a document that I hadn't taken into account before and is shown to me later, it can refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, one of the reasons that I've been asking you about Exhibit 1723, and that's your number 455-172/2 relates to General Pavkovic's report on the same matter the following day. And you know that exhibit, we've talked about it a lot in here, that's P1459, where he reported to the Supreme Command Staff about MUP's failure to be resubordinated to the army, right? You remember that one?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll recall when some of the witnesses for General Ojdanic were testifying there was a lot of discussion about their log-book and the archives and the documents indicating that General Ojdanic claims to not have received that document or seen it in 1999. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you may recall, I ask -- I think I asked another witness earlier about the timing of that document. Exhibit P968 in this case refers to the fact that on the 22nd of May it was made public the indictment regarding the Kosovo case, not the one in which you're named but those events, and that's only two days before you write your report about the MUP not being subordinated. Is that just a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity to follow those documents, if they had reached the army commander at that time, I mean the letter of Mrs. Louise Arbour, during the war I never heard of it or never seen it. So whether it's a coincidence or not, I cannot answer. You can look at it that way or another way. All I can say that at the time I didn't even know there was such a letter by Louise Arbour; I first heard it here in the courtroom. If I understood what you're asking, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, did you -- I guess my question is: The original order to subordinate the MUP came down about, I don't know, five weeks earlier, four, four and a half weeks earlier. Why did it take so long before you felt it necessary to write a report about its failure? Did anyone tell you to write it on that date or was that your own idea?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered that question in the examination-in-chief, but I'll repeat it now. At that time, a day or two before that document of mine, I received a written document and request of the 37th Motorised Brigade commander regarding failure to resubordinate and the resulting problems. Before that, we all knew that there was a failure to resubordinate, and we know that it was not the first report about it. We saw many other in the courtroom, but I decided to make a written report as well and to send people to check out that the problems indicated in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now that you say that, General, I do recall you mentioned it was that report from the 37th Motorised Brigade commander that you found alarming. Did your lawyer show you that document here in the courtroom? Have we seen that report here from the 37th commander?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have not yet admitted into evidence a document of similar contents through my testimony, but I expect that the brigade commander will come to testify; and when he does, part of those documents will be admitted through him and the brigade commander himself will be able to answer specific questions himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall now the date of that document, that report?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, between the 20th and the 23rd or maybe 22nd May. He wrote quite a lot, once in two, once in three days to report some problems, maybe I wasn't accurate enough, but at any rate on the 20th or after the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the commander of the 37th Brigade at that time -- was this Colonel Dikovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned when we were talking about your whereabouts in late April, you gave us some specifics. I want to ask you about document -- this is Exhibit Number 5D384. This is dated the 29th of April, and this also is in the 455 series, it's 455-196. Do you have that on the screen, General?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. This is very urgent and the first paragraph says: "At around 0900 hours on 29 April I personally came across a part of the 37th Motorised Brigade which was crossing a brook near Lozica village (next to the destroyed bridge) in disarray, while the commanding officer, in a passenger vehicle, had got stuck in the brook ..." Is that Dikovic you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've sent this document out. Did this go -- who did this go to? I don't see delivery information on it. Was this to all your subordinate commands?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two documents were written on the same day. They were sent with my signature, and I believe both were introduced into evidence during examination-in-chief, one was addressed to the commander of the 37th Brigade personally and another was sent to all units. The content was the same with minor modifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And although you didn't name him by name, any of those receiving this document would have known who the commanding officer of the 37th was, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commanders knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This would have been, don't you think, rather humiliating to him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war terrible things happen and everything is humiliating if it involves the death of soldiers. I would say that his soldiers were in danger of getting killed needlessly because they were taking the risk of inviting air-strikes, but it is not necessarily his fault. There was another of his men leading that column of soldiers. The brigade commander informed me later of all that. I would not use the word you used, humiliating, but I believe it was a problem and I drew the attention of the brigade commander himself and everyone else in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask, General, is that in Exhibit P2591, which we've seen before and I guess I'd like to bring it occupy now if we could. This is a document from Colonel Dikovic a few days earlier, I think the 25th of April. And this was a document that he sent to the Pristina Corps command, analysing the results of crushing the Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you've seen this document before, it was shown to someone earlier in this case. I'm waiting just a moment, General, to see the second page in English and direct you to the point I wanted to make that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He talked about the -- I think it's the third bullet point up from item number A. And I don't know if that's on your B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then we may need to go back a page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. He talked about: "Engagement of relatively large forces to fight small terrorist groups ('using an elephant to kill a fly')." Do you recall receiving that report?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the reports from that time but I remember this document because it has been shown at least twice here. I don't read all the reports. There is a team following reports and reporting, briefing about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't recall that you weren't annoyed at him for using that terminology to refer to the operations?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My engagement in that functional duty was not based on God knows which emotions. I taught that unit perhaps more often than I did others because it was outside the organic composition of the corps, it did not have any prior experience in anti-terrorist activities in 1998, it was located in the most hazardous part of the territory in the heart of Drenica, and I made personal efforts to boost the morale and build up their strength, that part of the brigade. I agreed that some of these statements are not militarily correct or fair, but still not enough for me to take it -- to hold it against him, that he's using his own initiative and thinking and suggesting ways and methods to facilitate command over units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, this looks on the face of it like a very wide-ranging criticism of the conduct of a campaign and includes a large number of specific criticisms about what was missing, like intelligence, communications equipment, training. Are you saying that this would be so filtered out by the system that you would not be aware of this complaint when you got the report from those in the corps responsible for monitoring reports and reporting to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I simplified things a bit to save time. I toured and checked that brigade, together with the army commander and another group of officers. What I'm trying to say is this was a young brigade commander who just came before the war to the area of Kosovo and Metohija and found himself at the deep end. I'm just trying to -- not to go into discussing all the bigger problems that this brigade had before their first baptism by fire when it started to carry out very serious tasks. It's true, some of those things that he says, the failure of communications and other problems, they persisted until the end of the war. We sent reinforcements, we sent even men from the army command who spent time with the brigade to help resolve the problem, so I'm aware of the problems. I'm not saying that the report is -- that that is not true; I'm speaking only about this specific report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about whether it was true or not. You've said that you don't recollect this report, and I wonder if that means that you were getting pretty much watered-down information about what was in the reports, since this one seems very specific, very wide-ranging, and very critical. I find it a little strange at the moment that you wouldn't be aware of it, whether it was true or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying in my answer that this report with this date, I cannot confirm having analysed myself. But as for the problems experienced by the brigade, beginning with the width of their zone and ending with the others stated here, I was aware of all that and I discussed it with the brigade commander personally. But I really cannot confirm that I had this report in my hands, this one with this specific date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to follow-up on that. I share some of what was just said by the Judge. It seems like -- I mean, these -- isn't this the kind of information that you were requesting from your subordinate units, an analysis of these actions so that you could use that information and make changes to do it better the next time? Isn't that one of the purposes of getting these kinds of reports?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a purpose, but by your leave, Your Honours, if we go to the action that ensued a couple of days later, it is explained that many of the things have been eliminated in relation to the experiences as they are set out in this document, but we will be able to see that through the testimony of General Nikovic. I know about other reports that are different to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that you would have seen this document, and the fact that you say now that you don't recall having seen it, there are a couple of possibilities. One is, as Judge Bonomy was suggesting, it was being filtered out. Were you subordinates trying to keep bad news from you? Do you have any reason to believe that or did you have any experience of that during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness has already given a clear answer to this question, to your question. I think that Mr. Lazarevic said that he knew about the complaints. I think that he did give quite a specific answer to you already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question that's been asked is a much wider question, and that is whether Mr. Lazarevic has experience of subordinate officers trying to conceal bad news from him, so he may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no such experience from any of the commanders. There were no bad news about any deaths and if this same commander could report to me that 12 of his people had been killed at one point and demand from me that the corps commander personally should come to the unit to assist. So we're talking about this commander quite specifically. So there's no reason for this commander not to send me other news that is far less negative. So this is specifically what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, one other possibility for you not remembering it, if you did see it in 1999, is that you were routinely getting these kind of reports with these kind of complaints and this one just is forgotten because it was routine. That's not the situation, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I've already said with an addition. There are no routine tasks in the defence of the country; and secondly, if I had wanted to read the reports, I would have been a military analyst, I would have been hiding in a shelter somewhere reading reports. I had to control, I had to direct, I had to command, I had to assist, and I had to try and be wherever I needed to be from the security point of view. This was my job as an officer, as a soldier. There was a duty operations team, duty officer's team, that analyses all the documents, writing reports, sending these reports on. Whenever it was necessary, short briefings were held to inform people. This was not as a situation that we have at the highest level of the command. This is something that may happen once under this tree, once under that tree, a command is trying to keep everything in its hands, tries to communicate with all the commanders, keep in touch with them, learn what is going on, and in this chaotic situation in the war, this is the method of work and this is the only method that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you weren't reading these, who was? Surely somebody within your command was reading these things on a regular basis when they came in right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Let me tell you, the duty operations team was receiving the reports, analysing the reports, and was then putting together the reports of the corps for the superior command and also preparing reports to brief the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of those people? How many -- first of all, how many are we talking about? Is this a group of six? Eight? 20?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about several teams that were rotated every day. Every day there would be one team on duty. I mentioned some of those leaders in examination-in-chief, Colonel Simonovski, Tesic, Tomislav Jovic, so I gave you the names of three of those team leaders and they would have under them four or five persons, officers, who would then be doing that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you expect that one of those guys doing that job having read a report like this that is wide-ranging and detailed and critical of the operations to at least summarize that and bring it to your attention?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained a few seconds ago this is how it was done. At those short briefings whenever it was possible to put together at the command, when the security conditions allowed that. As a rule, the reports should have come in by 1600 hours every day. They would be processed, and then between 19 and 2000 hours, if it was possible, a short meeting was held, it was chaired by me, at the corps command. And the next day, to analyse the events during the night, such a meeting would be held between 7.00 and 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think you've answered my question, though. Would you expect to be advised of this kind of thing by one of your subordinates responsible or reading those reports and briefing you at the end of the day? Wouldn't you expect this kind of thing to have been brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not claim that somebody had informed me or not. I just claimed that I had not held this report in my hands, and I would have expected the duty officer to tell me, to the extent that he was able to see the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall now having been advised of the substance of that report, even though you may not have ever held it in your hand?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in this sense, but in the sense that plans for a new action, counter-terrorist action, should be made for that area and that this brigade should be reinforced in order to be able to control the territory, that's definitely the case. And in that area there were two more subsequent actions in order to establish a fuller combat control of the territory and to reinforce that brigade. So in that sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, the reason I'm asking about this is because from the outside looking at the sequence and the events, it seems possible that when you came across then-Colonel Dikovic stuck in the creek, took a little pleasure in that and didn't mind mentioning the commanding officer of the 37th Brigade specifically in this warning to other units. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was looking at the Prosecutor very carefully, I was following what he said, but I really couldn't understand. Maybe the interpretation was not good, but could I please ask you to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm suggesting that on the 29th of April when you saw Colonel Dikovic stuck in the creek, this is the guy that I think your earlier description could be reduced to saying he was a bit brash, a bit of an upstart. He has filed this analysis or reported this analysis which is critical, very critical, of the operation. I'm thinking that this is in your mind at the time you see him stuck in the creek, and that's a very good example to bring to your troops and it didn't hurt -- you didn't mind mentioning him maybe a little humiliation would be good for him. Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm ready to accept responsibility for my failure to be specific enough, but I did not find Colonel Dikovic in such a situation that was causing a risk to his troops. I saw a reserve officer, not Dikovic, and that's what it says in the document. I didn't mention Dikovic at all, but I sent a warning to him as the commander, telling him that I had found a part of his unit in such a situation and that is the gist of this written document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, there must have been a misunderstanding I thought I tried to ask a specific question about that earlier and I understood your answer then to be that yes, he was the one. Are you telling me now that was wrong?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, I understand the Prosecutor to be asking me whether the commander of that brigade was Dikovic and I said yes, he was. But not that Dikovic was stuck in this creek with a car and with the aeroplanes about to attack his troops. We have a contemporaneous document which indicates all that quite clearly, and we have his report that followed after all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't clear to me because I asked you whether or not, wasn't it true that any of the -- any of the recipients of this warning or whatever we should call it would be aware of who that individual was, that commanding officer in a passenger vehicle, and you told me: "Yes, and if that's not Dikovic, who is it?"

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't follow the transcript. I didn't get an interpretation that would indicate that the question was whether Dikovic was in that car or not. I didn't understand it that way, and for the third time let me say quite in no uncertain terms that was not Dikovic. I didn't know that officer. I asked them what unit they were from and that's how I know they were from the 37th Motorised Brigade, and that is why I fired off this rather harsh warning demanding a report. We tendered this into evidence, and as you can see the brigade commander refers to what I had personally seen and warns his units accordingly. He doesn't say anywhere that I had found him in the creek.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, General--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since it's absolutely clear in the English translation that you did say that it was Dikovic you were talking about, we shall order that the B/C/S tape for today be listened to and that the passage at 67, 2, to 67, 11, should be re-interpreted. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, can you tell us where the 125th Motorised Brigade was located on the 28th and 29th of April, 1999, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 125th Motorised Brigade was in the area of the defence of the state border, to the right was the border with Montenegro, and to the left was Junik and some areas a little bit closer to Djakovica, and then in the depth -- the depth was about 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the commander was Colonel Zivanovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The incident in the creek that we were just talking about, you mentioned in that document that that was near Vozica [as interpreted] village. Can you tell us what that's near. I looked on my map to find one, but I'm not sure if I found the right one. Do you recall what other towns that was near?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Vozica, it's not Loznica, it's Lozica as far as I can recall from the document it's Lozica, and as far as I can recall it is to the north of the Pristina-Klina axis in the direction of Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we show you, General, Exhibit P615, this is our Kosovo atlas, and I believe it will be on page 18 in e-court. If we could scroll down to the lower left corner of that map and enlarge that. I'm actually looking for the area in block N17, so I think we need to move to the left and down, a little farther to the left. Do you see in the lower left corner there is something that appears to be Lozica on that map?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that the village you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, it might very well be the village. If this is the main road from Pristina to Klina, which I can't see now, but it's quite possible. At any rate, it is on that particular axis because I can see that Glogovac is to the north-east. This was a part of the area held by the 37th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would it help if we zoomed out then to see the wider area here? I think it's between -- well, roughly between Glogovac and Malisevo. You see the railroad line from Glogovac. Does that help orient you, General?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. It's not Malisevo. Malisevo is on the other side. This thick line in the lower area, that's the road and railway line Pristina-Klina-Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How far is -- would Lozica be from Djakovica, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 60 kilometres or more, maybe even less. If I could look at the map then I could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 125th Motorised Brigade was taking part in an action called the Reka action, which was completed on the 28th of April, correct? You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from the documents that were exhibited at this trial. But when we're talking about 125th Brigade, we're talking about the element that was resubordinated to it from the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you visited the 125th Brigade on the 29th of April, 1999, didn't you, with -- along with your --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where precisely did you tour or visit the 125th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, those were the positions between Decani and Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you narrow it down any more for us? Are you saying you visited several part of that brigade in several locations between Decani and Pec or did you just go to the headquarters? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander was there waiting for me at the positions of the armoured battalion that was closer to Pec, and then in this first zone visit we visited some units because the tour lasted several hours and we ended the tour in the brigade command. And there with him was the Chief of Staff who had come from the forward command post of the corps for us to visit those positions together, the ones facing the state border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you ended the tour in the brigade command, where was the brigade command located on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, in the outskirts of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where did you go after your visit to the 125th Motorised Brigade on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to the main command post, that was in the afternoon. I took the Decani-Klina-Pristina road to get to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So your best recollection is that you were in Pristina on the night of the 29th?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 28th, in the morning, we moved and we didn't stay there more than two or three days -- two days in fact. It seems to me that on the very next day, the 30th, the 31st, the 1st perhaps, that reconnaissance was carried out for the next command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe there's a translation problem. I'm confused on that. You say "on the 28th, in the morning, we moved ..." Where were you on the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th April, the command, and I together with it, we were -- from the 27th and -- to the 28th we were in the Tisnica [as interpreted] mine area; the 27th to the 28th, that was when we moved to Pristina; on the 28th in Pristina, we established a command post, we set up the communication lines with our subordinates. I visited some of the elements in Pristina, those that were supposed to carry out surveillance of the air-space, and I think there was a delegation of some women Kolo Srpskih Sestara, who had brought in some aid for the troops. I really don't remember everything that happened on the 28th but those were the activities. They were actually quite peculiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us again, because it's not clear in the transcript, from the 27th to the 28th where were you located?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moving of the command post from the Tisnica sector to a part of Pristina, near the law school or the school of economics to one or two buildings there. In the morning of the 28th, I visited two or three elements, those that were deployed in Pristina as a garrison element, including an element for automatic surveillance of the air-space. It's a group that -- it was a group that carried out radar surveillance of the air-space. And then the leader of that group in Pristina asked me to visit that element, and it seems to me it was on that day, that I did briefly talk to a group of people who had brought in some aid for the troops and that is called Kolo Srpskih Sestara.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me where the Tisnica sector is, that's your answer in line 24 of page --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kisnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you spell that for us.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kisnica, K, not T but K, Kisnica. It's to the west of Pristina in the direction of Gracanica, the Gracanica lake, and further on to Kosovska Kamenica, Kosovsko Pomoravlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the law school. General, I'd like to show you Exhibit P1492. This is an order from the Supreme Command Staff. I believe it's the 12th of May, 1999, and it's an order about moving VJ command post or units out of school buildings. Were you aware of that order? You may not have seen the Supreme Command Staff order. Did you get word of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see this order. I saw an order from the 3rd Army command and I issued my own order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To the same effect, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's 7.00. May we break for the evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may take up two minutes of your time. First of all, I owe you a report on the status of translation. My case manager tells me that yesterday he received an e-mail from the CLSS, informing him that the translation -- translations from the updated General Lazarevic list, that all of this has been completed. He sent the remainder of the documents to the CLSS, and 15 of those documents have already been translated. And I think that my colleague Mr. Cepic will be contacting Mr. Hannis about reducing the number of documents and updating the list, but at any rate 15 of the documents have already been translated. This is one thing. So -- but unless you have anything to say in this regard, I just wanted to ask one more question. It is impossible for me to calculate the time accurately, but it seems to me that Mr. Hannis is nearing the end of the time that was allotted to us for the examination-in-chief in his cross-examination. So perhaps he may want to share his position on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're able to assist us, Mr. Hannis, it no doubt helps Mr. Bakrac to programme the arrival of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm tired. I'm sure the General's tired of me as well. I'm going to try to finish in two hours tomorrow because I think that will put me about equal with the time that was spent on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there you have as clear an indication as you can get, Mr. Bakrac, and we are pleased to note what you say about the translations; but it's important that you keep CLSS fully occupied every minute of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that there is a possibility of sitting on Thursday morning rather than afternoon. I think another trial has been adjourned for the rest of this week. Is it inconvenient to change to the morning on Thursday for anyone? Well, in that event, if we can arrange it, we will sit on 9.00 on Thursday; but for tomorrow, it will remain at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of November, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
